title: Relational Database
subtitle: Tables, keys, SQL and Azure relational services in plain language.

what.body: Relational data lives in tables linked by keys, guarded by rules, and queried with SQL. If the data has a stable shape and relationships — customers, orders, employees — this is the model.
what.example: Customers holds each shopper once. Orders holds every purchase plus the shopper's CustomerID. That one shared ID connects the whole business.

concepts.body: Table = one entity type. Row = one record (one customer). Column = one attribute (City) with a data type.
Uniquely identifies each row: unique and never NULL. CustomerID and OrderID are classic examples. City or Name are not — they repeat.
A column referencing another table's key. Orders.CustomerID points at Customers.CustomerID and ties the two tables together.
One customer, many orders. The most common relationship: the 'many' side carries the foreign key.
Students take many courses; courses hold many students. A bridge table (OrderItems) stores the pairings.
No dangling references: an order may not point to a customer that does not exist. This is why deletes can be blocked.
Store each fact once and reference it. Customer details live in Customers, not copied into every order. Trade-off: more JOINs at query time.
SELECT reads · INSERT adds · UPDATE changes · DELETE removes · CREATE defines objects · ALTER redefines them.
WHERE filters rows · JOIN merges related tables · GROUP BY aggregates per group (with SUM/COUNT) · ORDER BY sorts.

View = saved query as a virtual table. Index = faster lookups, costs storage + write overhead. Stored procedure = saved SQL logic. Constraints (PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK) enforce rules.

examples.title: Two tables, one link
examples.body: CustomerID appears once in Customers and many times in Orders — that is the relationship.

examples.title: Normalization in one move
examples.body: Before: phone number copied into 1,000 order rows — one change means 1,000 edits. After: phone stored once in Customers, orders reference CustomerID. One edit, always consistent.

examples.title: Read this query
examples.body: SELECT * FROM Customers WHERE City='Bhubaneswar' — SELECT reads, * means all columns, WHERE keeps only matching rows.

services.name: Azure SQL Database
services.when: You want SQL without managing servers or the OS.
services.scenario: A startup's order system, online in minutes.

services.name: Azure SQL Managed Instance
services.what: Managed SQL with near-full Server compatibility.
services.when: Migrating a legacy app that needs broad compatibility.
services.scenario: Moving the company ERP to Azure almost unchanged.

services.name: SQL Server on Azure VMs
services.what: SQL Server you install on your VM.
services.when: You need OS-level control or exact version behavior.
services.scenario: An app requiring a specific SQL Server patch and custom agents.

services.name: Azure Database for PostgreSQL / MySQL
services.when: The app explicitly requires that engine.
services.scenario: A Django app that only speaks PostgreSQL.

remember: Row = one record · Column = one attribute · PK = unique + NOT NULL · FK = points elsewhere.
One-to-many carries the FK on the 'many' side; many-to-many needs a junction table.
SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE + WHERE/JOIN/GROUP BY/ORDER BY answer most syntax questions.
No WHERE on UPDATE/DELETE can hit every row — the exam's favorite trap.
Managed + compatible = Managed Instance · Managed + simple = SQL Database · Control = VM · Engine required = its managed offering.

quickCheck.q: Can City be a good primary key?
quickCheck.a: No — many customers share a city, so it is not unique.

quickCheck.q: Deleting a customer fails. Likely cause?
quickCheck.a: Orders still reference them — referential integrity blocks orphans.
GROUP BY region plus SUM — grouping with an aggregate.

quickCheck.q: Index on every column — good idea?
quickCheck.a: No — indexes cost storage and slow down writes.
